tools.title: What Did the Interview Actually Tell You?
tools.summary: An interview observes behavior. Hiring predicts future work. What connects the two?

examples.name: ML evaluation
examples.scenario: You’re hiring an ML engineer who will help decide whether models are ready to ship. You show a fraud-detection model with 92% accuracy and ask whether to deploy it. The candidate warns of possible data leakage: the test might use later customer disputes to predict whether an earlier payment was fraudulent. Those disputes would not yet be known when the model checks a new payment, so the test score could be misleading.
examples.impression: “They spotted leakage. They have good evaluation judgment.”
examples.tension: That could be true. But naming a familiar problem and knowing what to do about it are different pieces of evidence.
examples.comparisonTitle: What happens after they name the problem?

comparison.label: What happened
values: They mention possible leakage, then recommend deploying because 92% sounds high.
They ask whether the test used information available at payment time, propose retesting with only that information on later payments, and hold off on recommending deployment until that check is done.

comparison.label: What this supports
values: In this answer, they recommended release without resolving a risk they had identified. That raises a specific concern about their use of evaluation evidence. You don’t yet know how they would respond to guidance.
They connect a concern to a test and a release condition. That supports a more specific expectation: they may question an unreliable evaluation before recommending release.

examples.takeaway: When they name the risk, they set aside an identified concern when recommending release. When they act on the risk, they turn that concern into a check before release. These are different observations about judgment in this discussion. Whether the candidate can revise their reasoning with guidance or apply it to a new problem remains uncertain.

discussionCases.label: They name the risk
discussionCases.boundedConclusion: “They identified possible leakage but recommended release without resolving it. That raises a concern about how they used evaluation evidence in this answer. I’d need to see them address that concern before trusting a release recommendation. I don’t yet know how they would revise their reasoning with guidance.”
discussionCases.followup: Ask what information would be available when a payment arrives, and what test result would change their recommendation. Note any hints you provide and whether they use them.

discussionCases.label: They act on the risk
discussionCases.boundedConclusion: “In this case, they proposed retesting with information available at payment time and waiting for that result before recommending release. I’d expect them to contribute to model reviews, with help on our domain’s metrics. I haven’t yet seen whether they do the same with an unfamiliar problem.”
discussionCases.followup: Give them a different evaluation scenario and ask what would make them change their recommendation. Look for whether they adapt the reasoning rather than repeat the same test.

examples.name: System design
examples.scenario: You’re hiring a backend engineer to work on a service that uses a message queue. The candidate hasn’t used your queue product. A queue may deliver the same payment request more than once; without a safeguard, that could charge a customer twice. You still need to understand whether they can reason about failures, repeated messages, and recovery.
examples.impression: “They don’t know our stack. They’ll struggle with reliability.”
examples.tension: Unfamiliarity with a product is visible. Their ability to reason about reliability needs its own evidence.
examples.comparisonTitle: Two different reasons you might lack confidence
columns: You observed a problem in the reasoning

comparison.label: What happened
values: You asked which queue products they had used, but never discussed delivery failures or repeated messages.

You explained that the queue can deliver a message more than once. Even after discussing the consequences, they kept a design that could charge the customer twice and offered no way to prevent or detect it.

comparison.label: What this supports
values: You know they lack experience with this product. You don’t yet know how they reason about these failures.
You have evidence of difficulty handling this failure mode in this discussion. The concern is more specific than unfamiliarity with the product.

examples.takeaway: An interview that never tested failure handling leaves a question open. An answer that overlooks a failure after it has been explained gives you something concrete to examine. Neither warrants a broad claim about every aspect of the candidate’s ability.

conditions.label: What the interviewer supplied matters.
conditions.text: When you observed a problem in the reasoning, you had explained repeated delivery. Assess how they used that explanation; this does not show whether they would have identified the risk independently.

conditions.label: The role changes the forecast.
conditions.text: Judge the answer against the role’s responsibilities and the support the team can provide.

discussionCases.label: You haven’t tested the capability
discussionCases.boundedConclusion: “They’ll need to learn our queue. Before judging their reliability skills, I’d discuss a repeated-payment scenario and ask how they would prevent charging a customer twice. Product experience and failure reasoning are separate questions.”
discussionCases.followup: Explain the delivery behavior without requiring product-specific vocabulary. Ask them to trace one message through a failure and recovery. Then assess the reasoning against the role’s expectations.

discussionCases.label: You observed a problem in the reasoning
discussionCases.boundedConclusion: “After duplicate delivery and its consequences were explained, they kept a design that could charge a customer twice. For a junior role with design reviews, I’d expect them to need guidance on this failure mode. For a senior role leading payment design, this raises a stronger concern. I haven’t yet established whether this is a local gap or a broader difficulty.”
discussionCases.followup: Give targeted feedback and ask them to revise the design, then trace a repeated message through failure and recovery. This checks how they use support. A similar, unfamiliar scenario can separately test whether the reasoning transfers.

discussion.label: Evidence
discussion.question: What did we observe?
discussion.explanation: Describe the action or answer before giving it a meaning.

discussion.label: Expectation
discussion.question: What work might they handle, with what support?
discussion.explanation: Translate the observation into a specific work expectation. Name the help it assumes.

discussion.label: Uncertainty
discussion.question: What remains untested, and how would we check it?
discussion.explanation: Name the limit of the prediction and a next step that could change your confidence.

related.title: Decision-Complete
related.reason: Inspect the path from evidence to judgment.

related.title: From Intuition to Argument
related.reason: Turn a broad impression into a claim others can examine.

tools.discussionTemplate: We observed [specific behavior]. This suggests [a specific expectation or concern] about [work], given [conditions and support]. We’re still unsure about [gap], which we could check by [next step].
introduction: A technical interview shows how someone responds to a particular problem. Hiring asks us to predict their contribution on real work, with our team’s support and constraints.
The jump from an encouraging answer to a broad expectation can hide assumptions. Separate what you saw, what it suggests, and what remains untested.

lessons.title: Look for consequences.
lessons.text: When a candidate raises a concern, look at what happens next. A proposed check and a recommendation that depends on its result show more than naming the concern alone.

lessons.title: Identify the actual gap.
lessons.text: Not asking about a capability leaves it untested. Watching someone struggle after the problem is explained gives you a specific difficulty to investigate. These need different follow-ups.

lessons.title: Account for the prompt.
lessons.text: What the candidate demonstrated depends partly on what the interviewer explained, hinted at, or left unstated.

lessons.title: Keep predictions conditional.
lessons.text: One interview response does not establish performance across unfamiliar problems. Name the role, support, and conditions your expectation assumes so it can be questioned and revisited.

tools.insufficientEvidenceTemplate: We haven’t tested [capability], so we don’t yet have enough evidence to predict [how they would handle specific work]. We could check it by [next step].
tools.distinction: What you observed is evidence. What you expect them to do at work is a prediction. Keep the uncertainty visible.

tools.title: What Does This Result Let Us Decide?
tools.summary: Fewer overnight pages. A successful migration rehearsal. Both sound promising. What would you recommend next?
tools.cardSummary: An on-call engineer wants fewer overnight pages. A team wants to move its database. Explore what the results let them do next.
tools.problemTitle: The numbers look good. The next step is less clear.
introduction: A promising result arrives with a caveat. Is it a reason to stop, a reason to narrow the plan, or something to check before going further?
Follow two engineering decisions. In each one, change what the team knows or needs—and see why the recommendation changes.
tools.examplesDisclaimer: Two fictional situations. Explore the detail that changes each decision.
tools.discussionSummary: How this could sound in the report
tools.discussionTemplate: We found [result] on [cases]. That supports [interpretation], but leaves [gap]. Given [what the next step requires], I recommend [action and scope].

related.title: Decision-Complete
related.reason: Inspect the path from evidence to a defensible action.

related.title: What Did the Metric Throw Away?
related.reason: Ask whether an omitted distinction could change the choice.

examples.name: Overnight pages
examples.title: Fewer pages. Would the new rule still catch an outage?
scenario: It is 2 a.m. The on-call engineer gets another page from the checkout service. More than 1% of requests in the last five minutes have timed out. By the time they open the dashboard, the spike has passed.

The team has received 18 timeout pages in a week. Someone proposes raising the timeout threshold to 5%, keeping the same five-minute measurement window. Applied to last week’s traffic, that rule would have sent just four pages.
examples.impression: “Four pages instead of eighteen. Let’s raise the threshold.”
examples.tension: That would mean fewer interrupted nights. But would the new rule still wake someone when customers cannot complete a purchase?
examples.comparisonTitle: What did counting pages leave open?

comparison.label: Question
values: How many pages would the new rule send?
Would it still detect outages that need a response?

comparison.label: Finding
values: Four pages instead of eighteen on last week’s traffic.
During Thursday’s checkout outage, the highest timeout rate in any five-minute window was 3%. The proposed 5% rule would never have paged.

options.label: Only the number of pages
options.title: A quieter night is promising. Detection is still an open question.
options.evidence: The new rule would have sent four pages last week. Nobody has checked whether the pages it removes include incidents that needed a response.
options.recommendation: Keep the current rule for now. Replay known outages against the proposed threshold and check whether it would alert soon enough for the team to respond.
options.reason: The useful next check is about what the rule would miss. Another count of pages cannot answer that.
options.boundedConclusion: “The proposed threshold would reduce last week’s pages from 18 to 4. We have not checked which incidents it would miss. I recommend replaying known outages before changing the rule, because fewer interruptions only help if we still detect customer problems.”
options.followup: Replay known incidents and compare whether and when each rule would page. Inspect the incidents that would no longer trigger an alert.

options.label: They also replayed Thursday’s checkout outage
options.title: The quieter rule would have missed a real outage.
options.evidence: During Thursday’s checkout outage, the highest timeout rate in any five-minute window was 3%. Customers lost purchases, and the current 1% rule paged the engineer. The rate stayed below 5% throughout, so the proposed rule would not have paged at all.
options.recommendation: Do not adopt this threshold. Keep the current rule while looking for a way to filter brief spikes without hiding sustained checkout failures, then replay known incidents again.
options.reason: Fewer pages was a real improvement in one measure. The replay shows why that improvement does not justify this change.
options.boundedConclusion: “The proposed threshold would reduce last week’s pages from 18 to 4, but it would also miss Thursday’s checkout outage. I recommend keeping the current rule while we revise how it filters brief spikes. This threshold does not meet our need to detect sustained customer failures.”
options.followup: Revise the rule to distinguish brief spikes from sustained failures, then check it against known incidents before changing production alerts.

examples.takeaway: Fewer pages tells us about interruptions. To recommend this rule, we also need to know what happens to incident detection. Writing the recommendation exposes the part the first measurement did not answer.

examples.name: Migration scope
examples.title: The rehearsal passed. Why is the migration still on hold?
scenario: The team has spent weeks preparing to move its order database. In the rehearsal, recent orders arrive intact: totals match, relationships hold, and the application reads them correctly. The team wants to schedule the move.

Then someone asks about the archive. Older orders use a different schema, and none were included in the rehearsal. A colleague says the migration should stop until every historical format has been tested.
examples.impression: “We haven’t tested the archive. We can’t move anything yet.”
examples.tension: The gap is real. But does the archive have to move this weekend, or can it stay where it is while recent orders move first?
examples.comparisonTitle: The same rehearsal can support different migration plans

comparison.label: Requirement
values: The application can read recent and historical orders correctly from both databases. The archive stays available in the old system.
The application requires recent and historical records in the new database at the same time.

comparison.label: What the evidence supports
values: A staged migration of the tested record types, provided the application reads both databases correctly, the records remain consistent, and a safe way to undo the move has been tested.
The recent-record rehearsal does not establish that older schemas will migrate correctly. Test representative historical records before the full move.

interaction.question: What does the next move actually require?

options.label: The archive can stay; reading both databases and safely undoing the move have been tested
options.title: The archive can wait. A limited move has support.
options.evidence: The recent-order rehearsal passed. The team has also verified that the application can read orders correctly from both databases and that the move can be safely undone. Historical formats remain untested.
options.recommendation: Move the tested recent orders in stages and monitor the agreed checks. Keep the archive in the old database until its formats have been rehearsed.
options.reason: The gap limits which records can move. It does not, by itself, rule out the smaller move the team can safely support.
options.boundedConclusion: “The rehearsal supports moving the tested recent orders. The application can read orders correctly from both databases, and the team has tested a safe way to undo the move. I recommend a staged move while the archive stays in the old database. Historical formats still need their own rehearsal before they can move.”
options.followup: Monitor the agreed consistency checks during the staged move. Rehearse representative historical formats before expanding its scope.

options.label: The application needs all orders in the new database
options.title: This move needs evidence the rehearsal did not provide.
options.evidence: The recent-order rehearsal still passes. But the application cannot operate with the archive left behind, and historical formats remain untested.
options.recommendation: Hold the full migration. Rehearse representative historical formats, resolve failures, and verify the checks and a safe way to undo the move before scheduling it.
options.reason: The same caveat now concerns records required for the next step. It blocks this plan, even though the recent-order result remains valid.
options.boundedConclusion: “Recent orders passed the rehearsal, but the application requires the archive in the new database too. Historical formats have not been tested, so I recommend holding the full migration until that rehearsal passes and a safe way to undo the move has been verified.”
options.followup: Rehearse representative historical formats, resolve failures, and verify the complete move and a safe way to undo it before scheduling migration.

examples.takeaway: “The archive is untested” describes a limit of the rehearsal. Its consequence depends on the plan: it may restrict the move to recent orders, or prevent the full move from going ahead.

tools.endingTitle: What connects a result to a decision?
tools.ending: A measurement answers a particular question. A recommendation connects that answer to what the next step requires. Make the connection explicit, including what the evidence leaves open: the reader should be able to see why this action follows and where its support ends.
